claim: p53 is a potent suppressor of tumor growth.
source: The p53 transcription factor is a potent suppressor of tumor growth.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field stated in the abstract.

claim: Shortly after MDM2 inhibition by Nutlin-3, low levels of p53 rapidly activate approximately 200 genes.
source: Shortly after MDM2 inhibition by Nutlin-3, low levels of p53 rapidly activate ∼200 genes, most of them not previously established as direct targets.
evidence: This claim is supported by the GRO-seq experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Most of the approximately 200 genes activated by p53 after Nutlin-3 treatment were not previously established as direct targets.
source: Shortly after MDM2 inhibition by Nutlin-3, low levels of p53 rapidly activate ∼200 genes, most of them not previously established as direct targets.
evidence: This is based on comparison with published literature and databases of known p53 targets.

claim: The immediate p53 response upon MDM2 inhibition involves all canonical p53 effector pathways, including apoptosis.
source: This immediate response involves all canonical p53 effector pathways, including apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by functional annotation of the genes identified by GRO-seq.

claim: Microarray profiling fails to identify low abundance transcripts directly activated by p53.
source: Comparative global analysis of RNA synthesis vs steady state levels revealed that microarray profiling fails to identify low abundance transcripts directly activated by p53.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing GRO-seq results with microarray data.

claim: p53 represses a subset of its activation targets before MDM2 inhibition.
source: Interestingly, p53 represses a subset of its activation targets before MDM2 inhibition.
evidence: This is shown by comparing transcription levels in p53+/+ and p53-/- cells before Nutlin treatment.

claim: p53 regulates hundreds of enhancer-derived RNAs.
source: p53 regulates hundreds of enhancer-derived RNAs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GRO-seq analysis of p53 binding sites.

claim: Direct p53 targets harbor pre-activated enhancers highly transcribed in p53 null cells.
source: Strikingly, direct p53 targets harbor pre-activated enhancers highly transcribed in p53 null cells.
evidence: This is shown by analyzing eRNA transcription at p53 binding sites in p53-/- cells.

claim: In the absence of activating signals, p53 is repressed by the oncoproteins MDM2 and MDM4.
source: In the absence of activating signals, p53 is repressed by the oncoproteins MDM2 and MDM4.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the p53 field.

claim: MDM2 masks the transactivation domain of p53.
source: MDM2 masks the transactivation domain of p53 and is also an E3 ligase that targets p53 for degradation (Momand et al., 1992; Oliner et al., 1993; Kubbutat et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: MDM2 is an E3 ligase that targets p53 for degradation.
source: MDM2 masks the transactivation domain of p53 and is also an E3 ligase that targets p53 for degradation (Momand et al., 1992; Oliner et al., 1993; Kubbutat et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: MDM4 lacks E3 ligase activity but represses p53 transactivation potential.
source: MDM4 lacks E3 ligase activity, but represses p53 transactivation potential (Riemenschneider et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: p53 is inactivated in virtually all human cancers.
source: p53 is inactivated in virtually all human cancers, either by mutations in its DNA binding domain or MDM2/MDM4 overexpression.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cancer biology.

claim: p53 inactivation in cancers occurs either by mutations in its DNA binding domain or MDM2/MDM4 overexpression.
source: p53 is inactivated in virtually all human cancers, either by mutations in its DNA binding domain or MDM2/MDM4 overexpression.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cancer biology.

claim: Nutlin-3 binds to the hydrophobic pocket in MDM2 required for binding to p53, acting as a competitive inhibitor.
source: For example, Nutlin-3, the first-in-class compound, binds to the hydrophobic pocket in MDM2 required for binding to p53, thus acting as a competitive inhibitor (Vassilev et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: A comprehensive survey of the literature up to 2008 identified approximately 120 genes for which direct p53 regulation has been established.
source: A recent comprehensive survey of the literature identified ∼120 genes for which direct regulation has been established (Riley et al., 2008), but a comprehensive analysis of p53-regulated RNAs is still missing.
evidence: This is based on a cited literature review.

claim: Meta-analysis of four recent papers using ChIP-seq and microarray indicates that p53 may directly activate more than 1200 genes.
source: Meta-analysis of four recent papers using this strategy indicates that p53 may directly activate >1200 genes, yet only 26 of these genes were commonly activated in all four studies (Nikulenkov et al., 2012; Menendez et al., 2013; Schlereth et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2013) (see later, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on meta-analysis of published studies.

claim: Only 26 genes were commonly activated in all four recent ChIP-seq/microarray studies of p53 targets.
source: Meta-analysis of four recent papers using this strategy indicates that p53 may directly activate >1200 genes, yet only 26 of these genes were commonly activated in all four studies (Nikulenkov et al., 2012; Menendez et al., 2013; Schlereth et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2013) (see later, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on meta-analysis of published studies.

claim: Nutlin leads to p53-dependent transcriptional activation of hundreds of genomic loci prior to any significant increase in total p53 levels.
source: Strikingly, Nutlin leads to p53-dependent transcriptional activation of hundreds of genomic loci prior to any significant increase in total p53 levels, thus highlighting the critical role of MDM2 in masking the p53 transactivation domain.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GRO-seq and Western blot data.

claim: The lack of increase in total p53 levels upon Nutlin treatment highlights the critical role of MDM2 in masking the p53 transactivation domain.
source: Strikingly, Nutlin leads to p53-dependent transcriptional activation of hundreds of genomic loci prior to any significant increase in total p53 levels, thus highlighting the critical role of MDM2 in masking the p53 transactivation domain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Many p53 target genes transcribed at low levels are missed by microarray experiments.
source: Comparative global analysis of RNA synthesis by GRO-seq vs RNA steady state levels by microarray revealed that many p53 target genes transcribed at low levels are missed by microarray experiments.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing GRO-seq and microarray data.

claim: GRO-seq uncovered many gene-specific transcriptional events affecting key survival and apoptotic genes within the p53 network.
source: GRO-seq uncovered many gene-specific transcriptional events affecting key survival and apoptotic genes within the network, including the occurrence of bidirectional promoters (both overlapping and non-overlapping), clustered transactivation and various forms of antisense transcription.
evidence: This is based on analysis of GRO-seq data.

claim: Gene-specific transcriptional events in the p53 network include bidirectional promoters (both overlapping and non-overlapping).
source: GRO-seq uncovered many gene-specific transcriptional events affecting key survival and apoptotic genes within the network, including the occurrence of bidirectional promoters (both overlapping and non-overlapping), clustered transactivation and various forms of antisense transcription.
evidence: This is based on analysis of GRO-seq data.

claim: Gene-specific transcriptional events in the p53 network include clustered transactivation.
source: GRO-seq uncovered many gene-specific transcriptional events affecting key survival and apoptotic genes within the network, including the occurrence of bidirectional promoters (both overlapping and non-overlapping), clustered transactivation and various forms of antisense transcription.
evidence: This is based on analysis of GRO-seq data.

claim: Gene-specific transcriptional events in the p53 network include various forms of antisense transcription.
source: GRO-seq uncovered many gene-specific transcriptional events affecting key survival and apoptotic genes within the network, including the occurrence of bidirectional promoters (both overlapping and non-overlapping), clustered transactivation and various forms of antisense transcription.
evidence: This is based on analysis of GRO-seq data.

claim: GRO-seq revealed widespread activation of enhancer-derived RNAs (eRNAs) arising from p53 response elements.
source: GRO-seq revealed widespread activation of enhancer-derived RNAs (eRNAs) arising from p53REs.
evidence: This is based on analysis of GRO-seq data at p53 binding sites.

claim: Direct p53 target genes harbor 'pre-activated' p53 response elements, as defined by the strong production of eRNAs in isogenic p53 null cells.
source: Interestingly, direct p53 target genes harbor 'pre-activated' p53REs, as defined by the strong production of eRNAs in the isogenic p53 null cells.
evidence: This is based on analysis of eRNA transcription in p53-/- cells.

claim: After several hours of treatment with 10 μM Nutlin-3a, only p53 +/+ cells undergo cell cycle arrest.
source: After several hours of treatment with 10 μM Nutlin-3a (referred hereto as Nutlin), only p53 +/+ cells undergo cell cycle arrest and display induction of many known p53 target genes (Tovar et al., 2006; Henry et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: After several hours of treatment with 10 μM Nutlin-3a, only p53 +/+ cells display induction of many known p53 target genes.
source: After several hours of treatment with 10 μM Nutlin-3a (referred hereto as Nutlin), only p53 +/+ cells undergo cell cycle arrest and display induction of many known p53 target genes (Tovar et al., 2006; Henry et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: CDKN1A (p21) is a well-characterized p53 target gene.
source: Typical GRO-seq results are shown for two well-characterized p53 target genes, CDKN1A (p21) and TP53I3 (PIG3) (el-Deiry et al., 1993; Polyak et al., 1997), which display significant increase in GRO-seq signals upon Nutlin treatment only in HCT116 p53 +/+ cells (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: TP53I3 (PIG3) is a well-characterized p53 target gene.
source: Typical GRO-seq results are shown for two well-characterized p53 target genes, CDKN1A (p21) and TP53I3 (PIG3) (el-Deiry et al., 1993; Polyak et al., 1997), which display significant increase in GRO-seq signals upon Nutlin treatment only in HCT116 p53 +/+ cells (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: CDKN1A and TP53I3 display significant increase in GRO-seq signals upon Nutlin treatment only in HCT116 p53 +/+ cells.
source: Typical GRO-seq results are shown for two well-characterized p53 target genes, CDKN1A (p21) and TP53I3 (PIG3) (el-Deiry et al., 1993; Polyak et al., 1997), which display significant increase in GRO-seq signals upon Nutlin treatment only in HCT116 p53 +/+ cells (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, respectively).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GRO-seq data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The steady state expression of CDKN1A and TP53I3 mRNAs does not increase at the 1 hr time point used for GRO-seq.
source: Not surprisingly, Q-RT-PCR demonstrates that the steady state expression of the CDKN1A and TP53I3 mRNAs does not increase at the 1 hr time point as used for GRO-seq (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Q-RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A significant increase in the steady state levels of CDKN1A and TP53I3 mRNAs requires several hours of p53 activation.
source: In fact, a significant increase in the steady state levels of both mRNAs requires several hours of p53 activation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Q-RT-PCR data.

claim: 1 hr of Nutlin treatment does not increase total p53 or p21 protein levels to a significant degree.
source: Furthermore, Western blot analysis shows that 1 hr of Nutlin treatment does not increase total p53 or p21 protein levels to a significant degree (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Analysis of cell cycle progression using BrdU incorporation assays shows no signs of cell cycle arrest at the 1 hr time point.
source: Analysis of cell cycle progression using BrdU incorporation assays shows no signs of cell cycle arrest at the 1 hr time point, but a clear reduction in S phase cells is evident at 12 hr only in the p53 +/+ cells (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BrdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A clear reduction in S phase cells is evident at 12 hr of Nutlin treatment only in the p53 +/+ cells.
source: Analysis of cell cycle progression using BrdU incorporation assays shows no signs of cell cycle arrest at the 1 hr time point, but a clear reduction in S phase cells is evident at 12 hr only in the p53 +/+ cells (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BrdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Using the DESeq algorithm, 198 annotated gene loci were identified whose transcription is significantly induced upon Nutlin treatment in p53 +/+ cells.
source: Using a cut-off of adjusted p(a) <0.1, we identified 198 gene loci whose transcription is significantly induced upon Nutlin treatment in p53 +/+ cells (Figure 1D; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on DESeq analysis of GRO-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Only four gene loci showed transcription diminished in the p53 +/+ cells upon Nutlin treatment (FLVCR2, NR4A3, RELB and EGR1).
source: This analysis identified only four gene loci whose transcription was diminished in the p53 +/+ cells (FLVCR2, NR4A3, RELB and EGR1); however, none of these genes showed reductions in steady state mRNA levels upon prolonged p53 activation (see later, Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on DESeq analysis of GRO-seq data.

claim: None of the four genes with diminished transcription in p53 +/+ cells showed reductions in steady state mRNA levels upon prolonged p53 activation.
source: This analysis identified only four gene loci whose transcription was diminished in the p53 +/+ cells (FLVCR2, NR4A3, RELB and EGR1); however, none of these genes showed reductions in steady state mRNA levels upon prolonged p53 activation (see later, Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on comparison with microarray data.

claim: In p53 −/− cells, 5 genes were induced and 2 genes were repressed upon Nutlin treatment.
source: The specificity of Nutlin is demonstrated by the negligible changes observed in p53 −/− cells, where our analysis identified 5 induced and 2 repressed genes, all of which have less than 1.5-fold changes and none of which was among those differentially transcribed in p53 +/+ cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on DESeq analysis of GRO-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: All genes differentially transcribed in p53 −/− cells upon Nutlin treatment have less than 1.5-fold changes.
source: The specificity of Nutlin is demonstrated by the negligible changes observed in p53 −/− cells, where our analysis identified 5 induced and 2 repressed genes, all of which have less than 1.5-fold changes and none of which was among those differentially transcribed in p53 +/+ cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on DESeq analysis of GRO-seq data.

claim: None of the genes differentially transcribed in p53 −/− cells upon Nutlin treatment were among those differentially transcribed in p53 +/+ cells.
source: The specificity of Nutlin is demonstrated by the negligible changes observed in p53 −/− cells, where our analysis identified 5 induced and 2 repressed genes, all of which have less than 1.5-fold changes and none of which was among those differentially transcribed in p53 +/+ cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on DESeq analysis of GRO-seq data.

claim: Most of the 198 genes activated in p53 +/+ cells (176 out of 198) show an increase in transcription as early as 30 min after Nutlin addition.
source: The notion that these genes are indeed direct p53 targets is reinforced by the observation that most of them (176 out of 198) show an increase in transcription as early as 30 min after Nutlin addition to the cell culture (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on GRO-seq data at 30 min shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Of the 198 genes activated upon Nutlin treatment, 55 were known validated direct p53 targets.
source: Of these 198 genes, 55 were known validated direct p53 targets, 66 were targets predicted by one or more published microarray/ChIP-seq studies, and 77 are putative novel direct p53 targets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, a comprehensive annotation of these genes is provided in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on comparison with published literature shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Of the 198 genes activated upon Nutlin treatment, 66 were targets predicted by one or more published microarray/ChIP-seq studies.
source: Of these 198 genes, 55 were known validated direct p53 targets, 66 were targets predicted by one or more published microarray/ChIP-seq studies, and 77 are putative novel direct p53 targets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, a comprehensive annotation of these genes is provided in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on comparison with published literature shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Of the 198 genes activated upon Nutlin treatment, 77 are putative novel direct p53 targets.
source: Of these 198 genes, 55 were known validated direct p53 targets, 66 were targets predicted by one or more published microarray/ChIP-seq studies, and 77 are putative novel direct p53 targets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, a comprehensive annotation of these genes is provided in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on comparison with published literature shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Novel p53 target genes are induced at a 12 hr time point of Nutlin treatment at the mRNA steady state level to a degree comparable to genes predicted by published microarray/ChIP-seq studies.
source: Q-RT-PCR validation showed that novel genes are induced at a 12 hr time point of Nutlin treatment at the mRNA steady state level to a degree comparable to those genes predicted by published microarray/ChIP-seq studies (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Q-RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 12 out of 14 novel p53 target genes tested are also induced at the mRNA steady state level when using doxorubicin.
source: Furthermore, 12 out of the 14 novel p53 target genes tested are also induced at the mRNA steady state level when using doxorubicin, a DNA-damaging agent that activates p53 via stress signaling cascades (Lowe et al., 1994), thus revealing that transactivation of most novel genes is not unique to pharmacological inhibition of MDM2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Q-RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Transactivation of most novel p53 target genes is not unique to pharmacological inhibition of MDM2.
source: Furthermore, 12 out of the 14 novel p53 target genes tested are also induced at the mRNA steady state level when using doxorubicin, a DNA-damaging agent that activates p53 via stress signaling cascades (Lowe et al., 1994), thus revealing that transactivation of most novel genes is not unique to pharmacological inhibition of MDM2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is inferred from the doxorubicin induction data.

claim: Western blot analysis demonstrates protein induction for the novel genes GRIN2C, PTCDH4 and RINL upon Nutlin treatment.
source: Finally, we investigated whether activation of novel p53 targets can also be observed at the protein level. Indeed, Western blot analysis demonstrates protein induction for the novel genes GRIN2C, PTCDH4 and RINL (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: p53 directly activates a multifunctional transcriptional program at 1 hour of Nutlin treatment, including many canonical apoptotic genes.
source: p53 directly activates a multifunctional transcriptional program at 1 hour of Nutlin treatment, including many canonical apoptotic genes. See Supplementary file 1 for a complete list and annotation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1G and supported by functional annotation in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Flow cytometry analysis using the DO-1 antibody reveals increased reactivity as early as 1 hr of Nutlin treatment, indicative of unmasking of the p53 TAD1.
source: Flow cytometry analysis using the DO-1 antibody recognizing the MDM2-binding surface in the p53 transcactivation domain 1 (TAD1) reveals increased reactivity as early as 1 hr of Nutlin treatment, indicative of unmasking of the TAD1 at this early time point.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The DO-1 antibody recognizes the MDM2-binding surface in the p53 transactivation domain 1 (TAD1).
source: Flow cytometry analysis using the DO-1 antibody recognizing the MDM2-binding surface in the p53 transcactivation domain 1 (TAD1) reveals increased reactivity as early as 1 hr of Nutlin treatment, indicative of unmasking of the TAD1 at this early time point.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the DO-1 antibody.

claim: Among the induced genes identified by GRO-seq and microarray, only 102 are common.
source: Among the induced genes identified by the two experimental platforms, only 102 are common.
evidence: This is based on comparison of GRO-seq and microarray data.

claim: 291 genes are called as induced by the microarray experiment only.
source: 291 genes are called as induced by the microarray experiment only.
evidence: This is based on comparison of GRO-seq and microarray data.

claim: 72 genes were identified as induced by GRO-seq only.
source: Interestingly, 72 genes were identified as induced by GRO-seq only, despite the fact that the microarrays utilized harbored multiple probes against these mRNAs.
evidence: This is based on comparison of GRO-seq and microarray data.

claim: Microarrays detect 324 genes repressed upon 12 hr of Nutlin treatment.
source: Second, microarrays detect 324 genes repressed upon 12 hr of Nutlin treatment, none of which were called as repressed by GRO-seq.
evidence: This is based on microarray data analysis.

claim: None of the 324 genes repressed in the microarray were called as repressed by GRO-seq.
source: Second, microarrays detect 324 genes repressed upon 12 hr of Nutlin treatment, none of which were called as repressed by GRO-seq.
evidence: This is based on comparison of GRO-seq and microarray data.

claim: Nearly 40% of the 198 genes induced by GRO-seq harbor a p53 binding event within 25 kb.
source: Nearly 40% of the 198 genes induced by GRO-seq harbor a p53 binding event within 25 kb, significantly more than expected from random occurrence (p=1e−48, Hypergeometric test) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of p53 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The enrichment of p53 binding within 25 kb of genes induced by GRO-seq is significantly more than expected from random occurrence (p=1e−48).
source: Nearly 40% of the 198 genes induced by GRO-seq harbor a p53 binding event within 25 kb, significantly more than expected from random occurrence (p=1e−48, Hypergeometric test) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis using hypergeometric test.

claim: Among genes induced by microarray only, nearly 15% harbored p53 binding within 25 kb, significantly more than expected by chance (p=8e−11).
source: Among the genes induced by microarray only, nearly 15% harbored p53 binding within 25 kb, still significantly more than expected by chance (p=8e−11), which suggests that some of these genes may be true direct targets activated at later time points.
evidence: This is based on analysis of p53 ChIP-seq data and statistical testing.

claim: Genes considered as repressed by microarray profiling show little p53 binding within 25 kb, barely above what is expected by chance (p=3e−2).
source: Most importantly, genes considered as repressed by the microarray profiling show little p53 binding within 25 kb, barely above what is expected by chance (p=3e−2), suggesting that the repression observed is largely indirect.
evidence: This is based on analysis of p53 ChIP-seq data and statistical testing.

claim: The repression of genes observed in microarray profiling is largely indirect.
source: Most importantly, genes considered as repressed by the microarray profiling show little p53 binding within 25 kb, barely above what is expected by chance (p=3e−2), suggesting that the repression observed is largely indirect.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of p53 binding near repressed genes.

claim: GRO-seq identified 5 miRNAs directly transactivated by p53 (miR-1204, miR-3189, miR-34a, miR4679-1 and miR-4692).
source: Of note, GRO-seq identified 5 miRNAs directly transactivated by p53 (miR-1204, miR-3189, miR-34a, miR4679-1 and miR-4692, see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on GRO-seq data analysis.

claim: Nearly 72% of genes repressed in the microarray by Nutlin were previously shown to be downregulated upon overexpression of miR-34a in HCT116 cells (p<2.2e−16).
source: In fact, we found that nearly 72% of genes repressed in our microarray by Nutlin were previously shown by others (Lal et al., 2011) to be downregulated upon overexpression of miR-34a in HCT116 cells (p<2.2e−16, Hypergeometric test, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on comparison with published data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Ingenuity Pathway Analysis of genes repressed in the microarray experiment revealed that the top three regulators are E2F4 (p=1.02e−81), CDKN1A (p=8.21e−62) and RB (p=8.12e−60).
source: In agreement with these published findings, Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) of the genes repressed in our microarray experiment revealed that the top three regulators affecting these genes are indeed E2F4 (p=1.02e−81, Fisher's Exact Test), CDKN1A (p=8.21e−62) and RB (p=8.12e−60) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on IPA analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Most gene repression observed in the system is likely to be indirect, either via miRNAs such as miR-34a, and/or the p21>RB>E2F4 axis.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that most gene repression observed in our system is likely to be indirect, either via miRNAs, such as miR-34a, and/or the p21>RB>E2F4 axis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is inferred from the IPA and miR-34a overlap analyses shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: GRO-seq identified the transcriptional repressor PRDM1 (BLIMP1) as a direct target of p53.
source: Of note, GRO-seq also identified the transcriptional repressor PRDM1 (BLIMP1) as a direct target of p53 (Yan et al., 2007), revealing yet another possible mechanism for indirect gene repression downstream of p53.
evidence: This is based on GRO-seq data and cited literature.

claim: A small group of 'GRO-seq only' genes, including known p53 targets such as PTP4A1 and CCNG1, display very high basal steady state levels which do not increase significantly despite clear transcriptional induction.
source: This would explain why a small group of 'GRO-seq only' genes, including known p53 targets such as PTP4A1 and CCNG1, are not called by the microarray experiments: they display very high basal steady state levels, which do not increase significantly despite clear transcriptional induction (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing GRO-seq and microarray data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Most 'GRO-seq only' genes show very low levels of transcription and steady state mRNA expression.
source: However, most 'GRO-seq only' genes belong to a different category, as marked by their very low levels of transcription and steady state mRNA expression.
evidence: This is based on analysis of GRO-seq and microarray data.

claim: Genes like CDC42BPG, ADAMTS7 and LRP1 are clearly induced at the transcriptional level but show no apparent increase in microarray signals.
source: Genes like CDC42BPG, ADAMTS7 and LRP1 are clearly induced at the transcriptional level but show no apparent increase in the microarray signals (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing GRO-seq and microarray data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: The induction of low abundance 'GRO-seq only' genes upon p53 activation is evident by Q-RT-PCR at the time point of the microarray experiment.
source: Remarkably, the induction of these mRNAs upon p53 activation is evident by Q-RT-PCR at the time point of the microarray experiment (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Q-RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The 'GRO-seq only' group shows very significantly lower expression compared to all other groups in microarray-derived signals.
source: In fact, when microarray-derived signals are displayed for the various gene sets, the 'GRO-seq only' group shows very significant lower expression as compared to all other groups (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by box plot analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Microarray profiling is not sensitive enough to detect low abundance transcripts.
source: Altogether, we conclude that microarray profiling is not sensitive enough to detect these low abundance transcripts, which could explain why several published ChIP-seq/microarray studies failed to identify these genes as direct p53 targets.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of GRO-seq and microarray data.

claim: Clear p53 binding was detected to all p53REs tested at novel p53 targets.
source: Indeed, we detected clear p53 binding to all p53REs tested at these novel p53 targets (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-Q-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: p53 binds to proximal regions at the CDC42BPG and LRP1 loci (+1373 bp and −694 bp relative to TSS, respectively).
source: Of note, p53 binds to proximal regions at the CDC42BPG and LRP1 loci (+1373 bp and −694 bp relative to transcription start site [TSS], respectively), indicating that these genes could have been missed in previous studies due to the low abundance of their transcripts.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-Q-PCR data.

claim: p53 binds to very distal sites (>30 kb from the TSS) at the ADAMTS7, TOB1, ASS1 and CEP85L loci.
source: In contrast, p53 binds to very distal sites (i.e., >30 kb from the TSS) at the ADAMTS7, TOB1, ASS1 and CEP85L loci (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting that these genes would have been missed as direct targets when setting an arbitrary <30 kb window during ChIP-seq analysis.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-Q-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: GRO-seq enables the identification of novel direct p53 target genes due to its increased sensitivity and the fact that it does not require proximal p53 binding to ascertain direct regulation.
source: In summary, GRO-seq enables the identification of novel direct p53 target genes due both to its increased sensitivity and the fact that it does not require proximal p53 binding to ascertain direct regulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of GRO-seq with microarray and ChIP-seq approaches.

claim: In proliferating cells with minimal p53 activity, p53 increases the basal expression of some of its target genes.
source: Others and we have observed that in proliferating cells with minimal p53 activity, p53 increases the basal expression of some of its target genes (Tang et al., 1998; Espinosa et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: p53 status exerts differential effects among its target genes prior to MDM2 inhibition with Nutlin.
source: Interestingly, p53 status exerts differential effects among its target genes prior to MDM2 inhibition with Nutlin.
evidence: This is based on analysis of basal transcription in p53+/+ vs p53-/- cells.

claim: Many p53 target genes show increased basal transcription in the presence of MDM2-bound p53 (e.g., GDF15, DDB2).
source: While many genes show the same behavior as CDKN1A (e.g., GDF15, DDB2, labeled green throughout Figure 3), another group shows decreased transcription in the presence of MDM2-bound p53 (e.g., PTP4A1, HES2, GJB5, labeled red throughout Figure 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GRO-seq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Another group of p53 target genes shows decreased transcription in the presence of MDM2-bound p53 (e.g., PTP4A1, HES2, GJB5).
source: While many genes show the same behavior as CDKN1A (e.g., GDF15, DDB2, labeled green throughout Figure 3), another group shows decreased transcription in the presence of MDM2-bound p53 (e.g., PTP4A1, HES2, GJB5, labeled red throughout Figure 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GRO-seq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The differential behavior of RNAPII at basally activated and basally repressed gene loci is also observed in ChIP assays using antibodies against S5P- and S2P-RNAPII.
source: The differential behavior of RNAPII at these gene loci is also observed in ChIP assays using antibodies against the Serine 5- and Serine 2-phosphorylated forms of the RBP1 C-terminal domain repeats, which mark initiating and elongating RNAPII complexes, respectively (S5P- and S2P-RNAPII, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The differential effects of p53 on the basal transcription of its targets are generally translated into differences in mRNA steady state level.
source: Importantly, Q-RT-PCR shows that the differential effects of p53 on the basal transcription of its targets are generally translated into differences in mRNA steady level (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Q-RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ChIP assays show a significant amount of chromatin-bound p53 above background levels at the p53REs in the CDKN1A, PTP4A1 and HES2 loci, even before Nutlin treatment.
source: Importantly, ChIP assays show a significant amount of chromatin-bound p53 above background levels at the p53REs in the CDKN1A locus (basally activated), and the PTP4A1 and HES2 loci (basally repressed), even before Nutlin treatment (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The DO-1 ChIP signals increase upon Nutlin treatment, as expected from epitope unmasking.
source: Of note, the DO-1 ChIP signals increase upon Nutlin treatment, as expected from epitope unmasking.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP data.

claim: ChIP assays detect MDM2 chromatin binding above background levels at the p53REs in CDKN1A, PTP4A1 and HES2 loci, with signals decreasing upon Nutlin treatment.
source: ChIP assays also detect MDM2 chromatin binding above background levels at these three p53REs, with signals decreasing upon Nutlin treatment, as expected by the competitive action of this molecule (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Oncomine analysis of 598 cancer cell lines revealed that many genes basally activated in HCT116 cells such as CDKN1A, DDB2 and GDF15 show significantly higher mRNA expression in WT p53 cell lines.
source: Oncomine analysis of 598 cancer cell lines not treated with p53-activating agents revealed that many genes that are 'basally activated' in HCT116 cells such as CDKN1A, DDB2 and GDF15 indeed show significantly higher mRNA expression in WT p53 cell lines (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Oncomine analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The basally repressed gene GJB5 shows significantly higher expression in mutant p53 cell lines.
source: In contrast, the 'basally repressed' gene GJB5 shows significantly higher expression in mutant p53 cell lines.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Oncomine analysis.

claim: The direct p53 targets identified by GRO-seq are enriched toward the top of the ranking of genes by relative expression in WT p53 over mutant p53 cell lines.
source: Collectivelly, the direct p53 targets identified by GRO-seq are enriched toward the top of the ranking, which is revealed in a Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GSEA shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Genes induced only in the microarray platform (mostly indirect targets) do not show strong enrichment in a GSEA analysis.
source: In contrast, genes induced only in the microarray platform (i.e., mostly indirect targets) do not show strong enrichment in a GSEA analysis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GSEA analysis.

claim: The differential pattern of basal expression among p53 targets is also observed in an analysis of 256 breast tumors for which p53 status was determined.
source: Finally, the differential pattern of basal expression among p53 targets is also observed in an analysis of 256 breast tumors for which p53 status was determined, where CDKN1A, DDB2 and GDF15 (but not GJB5) show higher expression in the p53 WT tumors (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Oncomine analysis of breast tumors shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Key pro-survival genes such as CDKN1A, GDF15, BTG2 and MDM2 are transcribed at much higher rates than any apoptotic gene.
source: When direct p53 target genes with well-established pro-survival (i.e., cell cycle arrest, survival, DNA repair and negative regulation of p53) and pro-death (i.e., extrinsic and intrinsic apoptotic signaling) functions are ranked based on their transcriptional output in Nutlin-treated p53 +/+ cells, it is evident that key pro-survival genes such as CDKN1A, GDF15, BTG2 and MDM2 are transcribed at much higher rates than any apoptotic gene (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GRO-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Approximately 20-fold more RNA is produced from the CDKN1A locus than from the BBC3 locus encoding PUMA.
source: For example, ∼20-fold more RNA is produced from the CDKN1A locus than from the BBC3 locus encoding the BH3-only protein PUMA.
evidence: This is based on GRO-seq data analysis.

claim: The most potently transcribed apoptotic gene is TP53I3 (PIG3), yet its transcriptional output is still 3.4-fold lower than CDKN1A.
source: The most potently transcribed apoptotic gene is TP53I3 (PIG3), yet its transcriptional output is still 3.4-fold lower than CDKN1A.
evidence: This is based on GRO-seq data analysis.

claim: Differences in mRNA induction kinetics between gene classes could be explained from differential amounts of RNA synthesis.
source: Thus, differences in mRNA induction kinetics between gene classes could be explained from differential amounts of RNA synthesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the GRO-seq data showing differential transcriptional output.

claim: The basal activity of the CDKN1A locus is higher than most pro-apoptotic genes even in p53 −/− cells.
source: First, the basal activity of the CDKN1A locus is higher than most pro-apoptotic genes even in p53 −/− cells, which agrees with previous studies revealing the action of strong core promoter elements at this locus (Espinosa and Emerson, 2001; Morachis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GRO-seq data in p53-/- cells and supported by cited literature.

claim: p53 action leads to 'super-activation' (greater than fivefold) of the survival genes CDKN1A, GDF15, BTG2 and MDM2.
source: Second, p53 action reinforces the distinction between the two classes by leading to 'super-activation' (i.e., greater than fivefold) of the survival genes CDKN1A, GDF15, BTG2 and MDM2 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fold change analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: As a group, survival genes tend to be transcribed at a higher extent than apoptotic genes, which is due to a combination of p53-dependent and -independent mechanisms.
source: In sum, as a group, survival genes tend to be transcribed at a higher extent than apoptotic genes, which is due to a combination of p53-dependent and -independent mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of transcriptional output in p53+/+ and p53-/- cells.

claim: The promoters of survival genes carry more transcriptionally engaged RNAPII than the promoters of apoptotic genes.
source: GRO-seq confirms that the promoters of survival genes, including CDKN1A, indeed carry more transcriptionally engaged RNAPII than the promoters of apoptotic genes (Figure 4D); however, there was no obvious correlation between the amount of active RNAPII over the promoter and the degree of transcriptional output or induction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GRO-seq data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There is no obvious correlation between the amount of active RNAPII over the promoter and the degree of transcriptional output or induction.
source: GRO-seq confirms that the promoters of survival genes, including CDKN1A, indeed carry more transcriptionally engaged RNAPII than the promoters of apoptotic genes (Figure 4D); however, there was no obvious correlation between the amount of active RNAPII over the promoter and the degree of transcriptional output or induction.
evidence: This is based on analysis of GRO-seq data.

claim: RNAPII pausing is not a pre-requisite for rapid induction within the p53 transcriptional program.
source: Thus, RNAPII pausing is not a pre-requisite for rapid induction within the p53 transcriptional program.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of pausing indices shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There is no correlation between promoter divergence and fold induction among p53 target genes.
source: Using a 'divergence index', which evaluates the ratio of productive (sense) vs divergent transcription, we ranked p53 target genes from high to low promoter divergence, which revealed that there is no correlation between divergence and fold induction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The APAF1 gene is activated from a non-overlapping bidirectional promoter with the IKBIP gene, where the two start sites are less than 280 bp apart.
source: For example, the APAF1 gene, encoding a core component of the apoptosome, is activated from a non-overlapping bidirectional promoter with the IKBIP gene, where the two start sites are less than 280 bp apart (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GRO-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The FAS gene is transcribed from a bidirectional overlapping promoter with the ACTA2 gene, where the start site of one gene resides within the first exon of the other gene.
source: The FAS gene, which encodes a death receptor involved in p53-dependent apoptosis, is transcribed from a bidirectional overlapping promoter with the ACTA2 gene, where the start site of one gene resides within the first exon of the other gene, with the two transcription units overlapping for ∼850 bp (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GRO-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The TNFRS10 cluster encodes the pro-apoptotic TRAIL receptors DR4 (TNFRSF10A) and DR5/Killer (TNFRSF10B), as well as the counteracting decoy receptors DCR1 (TNFRSF10C) and DCR2 (TNFRSF10D).
source: One example is the TNFRS10 cluster encoding the pro-apoptotic TRAIL receptors DR4 (TNFRSF10A) and DR5/Killer (TNFRSF10B), as well as the counteracting decoy receptors DCR1 (TNFRSF10C) and DCR2 (TNFRSF10D) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GRO-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The pro-survival p53 target gene GPR87 is embedded within an intron of MED12L, which is not a p53 target.
source: One example of this scenario is the pro-survival p53 target gene GPR87, which is embedded within an intron of MED12L, which is not a p53 target (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GRO-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: GRO-seq readily detects RNAs originating from most p53 binding events.
source: GRO-seq readily detects RNAs originating from most p53 binding events, which we refer hereto as eRNAs.
evidence: This is based on analysis of GRO-seq data at p53 binding sites.

claim: A distal p53 binding site downstream of the DDIT4 gene is clearly transcribed in both the sense and antisense directions, with increased signals upon p53 activation.
source: A typical example is shown for the DDIT4 locus in Figure 5A, where a distal p53 binding site located downstream of the gene is clearly transcribed in both the sense and antisense directions, with increased signals upon p53 activation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GRO-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The p53RE downstream of DDIT4 is also transcribed in p53 −/− cells.
source: Interestingly, this p53RE is also transcribed in p53 −/− cells (Figure 5A, top track, arrow).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GRO-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Analysis of the CDKN1A locus shows transcription from the well characterized p53REs at −1.3 and −2.4 kb.
source: Analysis of the CDKN1A locus shows transcription from the well characterized p53REs at −1.3 and −2.4 kb (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GRO-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: lincRNA-p21 could be classified as an eRNA, as it originates from the vicinity of a p53RE associated to a canonical p53 target gene.
source: This suggests that lncRNA-p21 could be classified as an eRNA, as it originates from the vicinity of a p53RE associated to a canonical p53 target gene.
evidence: This is inferred from the GRO-seq data showing transcription from a p53 binding site.

claim: Transcripts derived from the lincRNA-p21 region can be detected in p53 −/− cells.
source: Once again, transcripts derived from the lincRNA-p21 region can also be detected in p53 −/− cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, top track).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GRO-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Direct p53 target genes display an enrichment in p53 binding close to promoters, but also within genes.
source: Analysis of the spatial distribution of p53 binding events relative to transcription start sites (TSSs) shows that direct p53 target genes display an enrichment in p53 binding close to promoters, but also within genes (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: It has been estimated that approximately 40% of p53 enhancers are intragenic.
source: In fact, it has been estimated that ∼40% of p53 enhancers are intragenic (Nikulenkov et al., 2012; Menendez et al., 2013; Schlereth et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on cited literature.

claim: p53 activation leads to antisense transcription within a large fraction of its direct target genes concurrently with activation of the protein-coding RNAs.
source: Thus, p53 activation leads to antisense transcription within a large fraction of its direct target genes concurrently with activation of the protein-coding RNAs, a phenomenon with potential regulatory consequences.
evidence: This is based on analysis of GRO-seq data showing intronic antisense eRNAs.

claim: Approximately 40% of distal p53 binding sites and those not associated with p53 targets are transcriptionally active in p53 −/− cells.
source: This revealed that ∼40% of distal sites and those not associated with p53 targets are transcriptionally active in p53 −/− cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The fraction of transcriptionally active p53 binding sites increases to approximately 60% in p53 +/+ cells.
source: The number increases to ∼60% in p53 +/+ cells, likely revealing the action of basal p53 levels, as observed for the DRAM1 locus.
evidence: This is based on analysis of eRNA transcription.

claim: When analysis is restricted to p53REs within 25 kb of a direct p53 target, the fraction that are transcribed in p53 −/− cells increases to approximately 70%.
source: When the analysis is restricted to those p53REs within 25 kb of a direct p53 target, the fraction that are transcribed in p53 −/− cells increases to ∼70%, and nearly all of them are transcriptionally active in Nutlin-treated p53 +/+ cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Nearly all p53REs within 25 kb of a direct p53 target are transcriptionally active in Nutlin-treated p53 +/+ cells.
source: When the analysis is restricted to those p53REs within 25 kb of a direct p53 target, the fraction that are transcribed in p53 −/− cells increases to ∼70%, and nearly all of them are transcriptionally active in Nutlin-treated p53 +/+ cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is based on analysis of eRNA transcription.

claim: eRNAs are a hallmark of active p53 binding sites.
source: Thus, eRNAs are a hallmark of active p53 binding sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis showing high transcription at active p53 binding sites.

claim: p53 stimulates eRNA transcription to a similar degree regardless of location.
source: A fold induction analysis shows that p53 stimulates eRNA transcription to a similar degree regardless of location (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fold change analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: eRNA transcription is much weaker from distal sites relative to proximal sites (p=1.28e−12 for Nutlin-treated p53 +/+ cells).
source: First, eRNA transcription is much weaker from distal sites relative to proximal sites (p=1.28e−12 for Nutlin-treated p53 +/+ cells).
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis of eRNA levels.

claim: eRNA transcription is significantly higher from proximal sites associated with direct p53 target genes.
source: Second, eRNA transcription is significantly higher from proximal sites associated with direct p53 target genes.
evidence: This is based on analysis of eRNA levels at different p53 binding sites.

claim: The difference in eRNA transcription between sites near p53 targets and sites near non-targets is already evident in p53 −/− cells (p=1e−10).
source: Strikingly, this difference is already evident in p53 −/− cells (p=1e−10).
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis of eRNA levels in p53-/- cells.

claim: A distinctive feature between direct p53 target genes and genes proximal to bound p53REs but not activated is the strength of eRNA production in the absence of p53.
source: Thus, a distinctive feature between direct p53 target genes and those genes proximal to bound p53REs but not activated is the strength of eRNA production in the absence of p53.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of eRNA levels in p53-/- cells.

claim: p53 seems to activate gene expression at genomic locations carrying 'primed', pre-activated enhancers, likely revealing the action of pioneer factors.
source: In other words, p53 seems to activate gene expression at genomic locations carrying 'primed', pre-activated enhancers, likely revealing the action of pioneer factors (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of high eRNA transcription in p53-/- cells at sites near p53 targets, as illustrated in Figure 5E.
